summaries.gardner: Lam is a top dog in etch and a deposition leader riding AI-driven chip spending, the stock more than doubled over the past year and many call it expensive, all Rule Breaker positives. It is less of a fit on consumer brand recognition and on being a newly emerging industry, since chip equipment is mature and cyclical.
summaries.buffett: Lam has a durable moat from tool-of-record switching costs, ROIC around 70% and strong free cash flow, much of it returned via buybacks and dividends. But its results swing with the chip cycle (revenue fell 14.5% in FY2024) and at about 50 times trailing earnings there is no margin of safety, so it is a quality business at a full price for a Buffett-style buyer.
summaries.munger: Munger would admire the hard-to-copy plasma know-how, high returns on capital and rational capital allocation. Inverting, the risks are clear but manageable: export controls on China (26% of June-2026 quarter revenue), memory-capex cycles and rival tool wins, and the current price leaves little room for error.
summaries.lynch: Lam fits Lynch's cyclical category with a simple story: more AI and memory chips need more etch and deposition steps. With a P/E near 50 on trailing and about 31 on forward earnings it is not cheap relative to long-run growth, and the stock is widely followed rather than overlooked; insiders have been selling while the company shrinks its share count.
summaries.fisher: Lam scores well on Fisher's points: a large runway in AI-era chip equipment, $2.38 billion of R&D in FY2026 that produces new platforms like Akara and panel packaging tools, rising margins and close customer relationships. A Fisher investor would accept the cyclicality for the long-term growth.
summaries.graham: Lam fails Graham's defensive-investor tests on price: about 50 times trailing earnings and roughly 29 times book value. It does pass on size, a strong balance sheet (cash exceeds debt, current ratio about 2.6) and continuous profitability, but its dividend record (initiated in 2014) is short of 20 years.
summaries.thiel: Lam is a near-monopoly in some niches such as high-aspect-ratio etch for 3D NAND, with proprietary process know-how and a direct sales and service relationship with every leading chipmaker. Its technology is not ten times better across the board, and it competes in a concentrated oligopoly rather than having created a new market.
summaries.gerstner: Lam benefits directly from the AI build-out, with consensus expecting about 50% revenue growth in FY2027 and earnings estimates rising, and it is very profitable with strong cash generation. Gerstner-style discipline would flag the high multiple and cyclical risk, but the growth-adjusted valuation on forward earnings is not extreme.
summaries.druckenmiller: Liquidity and the AI capex boom favor Lam: September-quarter guidance of $8.1 billion revenue and analysts lifting estimates fit Druckenmiller's focus on accelerating earnings. The stock has already doubled in a year and fell sharply from its July 2026 peak of about $438, so timing and sentiment risk are high.
summaries.smith: Lam meets Terry Smith's quality tests of high returns on capital (ROIC about 70%), high gross margins (50.5%) and strong cash conversion, but its cyclicality makes it less predictable than Fundsmith's staple holdings. At about 77 times free cash flow it fails the 'don't overpay' test today.
summaries.greenblatt: Lam's return on capital is excellent, but its earnings yield is low: operating income of $8.20 billion against an enterprise value of about $363 billion gives an EBIT/EV of about 2.3%. It would rank poorly on the Magic Formula at today's price.
summaries.akre: Lam has two legs of Akre's stool: an extraordinary business with high returns and talented management that reinvests and buys back stock well. The third leg, reinvestment opportunity at high returns, is decent but cyclical, and the price is far from the bargain Akre prefers.
summaries.pabrai: Pabrai's Dhandho approach seeks low-risk, high-uncertainty bets at deep discounts; Lam is a high-quality business but trades at about 50 times earnings after a 100%+ one-year rise, so it offers no 'heads I win, tails I don't lose much' setup today.
summaries.wood: Lam is an enabler of AI rather than a disruptive platform in ARK's sense: its tools help make AI chips and memory, but its costs are not collapsing along a Wright's-law curve and it does not combine multiple innovation platforms. It fits Wood's themes only indirectly.
summaries.ackman: Lam meets several Pershing Square criteria: a simple, predictable-ish, free-cash-flow-generative business with a moat, strong balance sheet and good management. Its cyclicality and current valuation work against Ackman's preference for predictable businesses bought at a discount to intrinsic value.
summaries.sleep: Nick Sleep would see a scale-economics element in Lam's growing installed base and service business, but Lam does not pass scale savings back to customers in the Costco/Amazon way; it uses its position to raise margins. Its long-term position looks solid, not clearly stronger in 10-20 years.
summaries.valentine: Valentine looked for huge markets and hard technology problems: Lam solves an essential, extremely hard problem in a $150+ billion equipment market riding AI. As a 1980-founded public incumbent it is outside his venture lens, but the market-first logic fits well.
summaries.nash: Lam passes many of Nash's quality screens: a real secular trend, 26% revenue growth in FY2026, 35% operating margin, more cash than debt, short interest around 2% and a scorecard total of 105. It fails on the CEO's tenure and insider selling, on five-year consistency (FY2024 dip), and on valuation, with Nash's 12% DCF giving about $88 per share versus about $291.

momentum.evidence: The stock closed near $141.51 in mid-October 2025 and traded at $290.64 on October 14, 2026, a gain of about 105% in a year, though it is down about a third from its July 2026 high of $438.50.

g4.evidence: CEO Tim Archer has delivered record margins, and about 88% of shares are held by institutions; its key partners are the world's top chipmakers (TSMC, Samsung, SK hynix, Micron).

g6.evidence: At about 50 times trailing GAAP EPS of $5.76 and 16 times sales, some commentators call it expensive, though most analysts rate it Strong Buy (25 Strong Buy, 4 Buy, 6 Hold in October 2026).

simple.evidence: The business model (sell chip-making tools then service them) is simple, but the plasma etch and deposition technology and memory-cycle dynamics take effort for a generalist to understand.

b2.evidence: Lam has been profitable every year with revenue rising from $14.63 billion in FY2021 to $23.23 billion in FY2026, but revenue fell 14.5% in FY2024 during the memory downturn.

integrity.evidence: Lam gives clear guidance and has consistently beaten it, and it returned $5.12 billion via buybacks and dividends in FY2026, but insiders including the CEO and directors have sold tens of millions of dollars of stock in 2026 and own only about 0.26%.

b6.evidence: Lam has avoided large acquisitions since buying Novellus in 2012 and focuses on organic R&D and buybacks.

roic.evidence: ROIC is about 70% (StockAnalysis), with cash of $5.58 billion exceeding debt of $3.73 billion at June 2026.

fcf.evidence: FY2026 free cash flow was $4.89 billion ($5.86 billion operating cash flow minus $0.97 billion capex), 67% of $7.27 billion net income, below the 101% conversion of FY2025 as receivables rose.

b10.evidence: Market value rose from roughly $82 billion in October 2021 (about $56 a share) to about $365 billion, far more than the earnings retained after dividends and buybacks.

safety.evidence: At $290.64 the stock trades about 50 times FY2026 EPS and well above a conservative DCF (about $88 per share using 3-year average growth and FCF margins at 12%).

fairprice.evidence: A forward P/E of about 31 on FY2027 consensus EPS of $9.48 (about 65% growth) looks reasonable for the growth, but trailing multiples of 50 times earnings and 77 times free cash flow are rich for a cyclical.

mu5.evidence: With entrenched tool-of-record positions, a large service base and a net cash balance sheet, permanent failure is unlikely; the main risks are cyclical downturns, China export limits and share loss at new nodes.

reinvest.evidence: Lam reinvests $2.38 billion a year in R&D at high returns, but capital needs are modest so most cash goes to buybacks and dividends rather than reinvestment.

ly2.evidence: It is a classic cyclical-growth stock: AI, high-bandwidth memory and 3D NAND layer counts drive more etch and deposition per wafer.

ly3.evidence: Trailing P/E of about 50 is above the long-run EPS growth (Simply Wall St forecasts about 21% a year), though the forward P/E of about 31 is below next year's expected 65% EPS growth.

runway.evidence: Consensus sees revenue rising from $23.23 billion in FY2026 to $47.7 billion by FY2029, and Lam says its served market per NAND wafer doubles moving from 128 to 500+ layers.

ly7.evidence: Diluted shares fell from 1,453 million in FY2021 to 1,261 million in FY2026 through buybacks, but insiders are net sellers, e.g. CEO Archer sold 30,000 shares at $319.26 about a month ago.

ly8.evidence: Lam is a $365 billion company covered by about 35 analysts and owned 88% by institutions.

fi2.evidence: Lam keeps launching new platforms such as Akara conductor etch for gate-all-around, ALTUS Halo molybdenum deposition and 310x310 mm and 510x515 mm panel packaging tools.

fi3.evidence: R&D of $2.38 billion in FY2026 produced tool-of-record wins (Akara's installed base doubling annually) and gross margin up to 50.5%.

fi4.evidence: Lam's sales and service model is deeply embedded with a few big chipmakers, with customer support revenue up 43% year over year to nearly $2.5 billion in the June 2026 quarter, but it is not known for exceptional salesmanship beyond engineering.

longterm.evidence: Lam kept R&D high through the FY2024 downturn and is building out new markets like advanced packaging and backside power.

gr1.evidence: Lam had $23.23 billion of FY2026 revenue and a market value of about $365 billion.

ni10.evidence: Lam has reported net income every fiscal year for more than a decade, including $3.83 billion in the FY2024 downturn and $7.27 billion in FY2026.

gr4.evidence: Lam started paying dividends in 2014, so it has about 12 years of dividends, short of 20.

eps10.evidence: Diluted EPS rose from $2.69 (split-adjusted) in FY2021 to $5.76 in FY2026, more than doubling in five years alone.

gr6.evidence: The price is about 50 times FY2026 EPS of $5.76, far above 15 times average earnings.

gr7.evidence: P/E of about 50 times P/B of about 29 (equity $12.47 billion) gives roughly 1,460, far above 22.5.

th1.evidence: Lam leads in high-aspect-ratio etch, but Applied Materials and Tokyo Electron have comparable technology in many steps; it is not ten times better.

timing.evidence: Lam raised its 2026 wafer-fab-equipment outlook to the low-$150 billion range in July 2026, with DRAM, NAND upgrades and advanced packaging all growing.

th3.evidence: Lam built a leading share in plasma etch and expanded into deposition (Novellus 2012) and clean, but its overall wafer-fab-equipment share is only around 10%.

team.evidence: Archer and CFO Doug Bettinger are respected operators with a strong record, but not an exceptional founder-led team.

th5.evidence: Lam's direct sales and field-service organisation is embedded in every major fab, generating nearly $2.5 billion of customer support revenue in the June 2026 quarter.

durable.evidence: Etch and deposition will remain essential for decades, but shifts in device architecture and Chinese competitors could change share at each new node.

th7.evidence: AI-driven chip-equipment demand is widely recognised by all equipment makers and investors.

trend.evidence: AI drives Lam's growth: NAND upgrades for enterprise SSDs, high-bandwidth memory, gate-all-around logic and advanced packaging expected to grow over 70% in 2026.

dr1.evidence: Quarterly revenue rose from $5.17 billion (June 2025) to $6.72 billion (June 2026) with guidance of $8.1 billion for September 2026, and FY2027 consensus EPS of $9.48 is well above FY2026's $5.76.

dr2.evidence: DRAM and NAND upgrade spending and advanced packaging could lift results further into 2027, but much of this is already in consensus estimates of about 50% revenue growth.

dr4.evidence: AI capex is strong, but export controls and high rates or a tech-spending pullback could hurt; the stock's beta is about 1.85.

dr6.evidence: Upcoming catalysts include the September-quarter report (expected around Oct 21, 2026), 2027 WFE outlook and panel-level packaging shipments.

dr7.evidence: Business quality supports conviction, but cyclicality, China exposure and a high multiple argue against a very concentrated position.

gm.evidence: Gross margin rose to 50.5% in FY2026 from 44.6% in FY2023, with 52% guided for the September 2026 quarter.

fcfyield.evidence: FY2026 free cash flow of $4.89 billion on a $365 billion market value is a yield of about 1.3%.

gb2.evidence: FY2026 operating income of $8.20 billion is about 2.3% of an enterprise value of about $363 billion.

pa2.evidence: The business is in an upswing (FY2026 revenue +26%); the recent share-price drop from $438 reflects sentiment rather than a business setback.

pa4.evidence: The business is unlikely to fail, but at about 50 times earnings the shares could fall far in a chip-equipment downturn, as in 2022 when they roughly halved.

wo1.evidence: Lam is a leading supplier of tools that make AI chips and memory, an enabler rather than an AI leader itself.

wo2.evidence: Lam's tool prices rise with complexity; gross margin increased to 50.5%, not falling costs opening new demand.

wo3.evidence: Lam serves semiconductor manufacturing only; it does not combine multiple innovation platforms.

wo4.evidence: Consensus sees revenue roughly doubling by FY2029 ($47.7 billion), not a many-times larger market in five years.

ns4.evidence: Rising etch/deposition intensity in AI chips may strengthen Lam, but Chinese rivals and new architectures make a clearly stronger position uncertain.

va2.evidence: Without precise etch and deposition, chipmakers cannot build 3D NAND, HBM or 2nm logic, a very large, painful problem.

tn1.evidence: Lam sells picks and shovels for the AI build-out (memory, HBM, gate-all-around, advanced packaging), an infrastructure layer, though it predates AI.

tn3.evidence: Lam is a large-cap US company and not a commodity producer, airline, seasonal business or startup, though it is cyclical.

tn4.evidence: Revenue grew in FY2025 and FY2026 (to $23.23 billion), it is highly profitable (31.3% net margin), and cash of $5.58 billion exceeds debt of $3.73 billion.

tn5.evidence: Free cash flow was positive in each of the last six quarters (e.g. $1.27 billion in the June 2026 quarter) and cash exceeded total debt at each quarter end.

tn6.evidence: FY2026 revenue grew 26.0%, and June-2026 quarter revenue grew 30% year over year.

tn7.evidence: FY2026 revenue growth of 26.0% plus free-cash-flow margin of 21.1% equals about 47.

tn8.evidence: In FY2026 revenue grew 26.0% while R&D plus SG&A grew 14.5% to $3.53 billion.

tn9.evidence: Market cap about $365 billion, cash above debt, short interest about 2.1%, operating margin 35.3%, revenue growth 26%, no recent earnings misses and founded in 1980.

tn10.evidence: US export controls on China (26% of June-2026 quarter revenue) are a significant regulatory risk, though no major litigation threatens the company.

tn11.evidence: Lam provides etch, deposition and clean tools that help chipmakers build smaller, denser chips, charging per tool plus recurring service, spares and upgrades, and wins on process performance and tool-of-record incumbency.

tn13.evidence: Total 105: cash vs debt 5, revenue growth 10, operating margin 10, short interest 10, institutional ownership 10, revenue faster than expenses 10, 5-year return vs S&P 10 (about +409%), moat 10, CEO 5, recession-proof pricing power 5, secular trend 10, culture and mission 5, talent 5.
